question: Not shared at the level of population class. Both papers detect current MCI against normal cognition from clinical and questionnaire tabular data, so the task, comparison and channel match. The populations behind the label differ in kind, as in C-180. P-343 studies hospitalised type 2 diabetes patients aged 40 or over in an endocrinology department (Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital), and the authors say the model is mainly applicable to older patients with poorer glycaemic control. P-19 studies working-age coal miners with occupational dust exposure attending an occupational health examination (inclusion age >= 18; mean 42.6 years normal / 48.8 MCI). The predictors are tied to each population (eGFR, systolic blood pressure, BMI, diabetes duration and a glucolipid 'GCA' index against work years, social support and anxiety), sharing only age and education. The MCI definitions also differ: AAN 2018 clinical criteria with a Beijing MoCA < 26 in P-343; a MoCA <= 26 screen alone in P-19.

figures.P-343: Internal (Table 2, tuned SVC): 0.74 +/- 0.04, where the paper says 'Confidence intervals were computed with the mean and standard deviation of the metrics during cross-validation' (the extract drops decimal points: '0 74 ± 0 04'). Read as mean +/- 1.96 SD: [0.662, 0.818]. Derived Hanley-McNeil at the 623-person validation split (about 218 MCI/405 NC at the text's 724/2074): Q1 = 0.5873, Q2 = 0.6294, SE^2 = 41.91/(218*405), SE = 0.0218, [0.697, 0.783] (Table 1's 784/1290 gives 235/388 and [0.698, 0.782]). External DECODE cohort (Table 3 SVC row; abstract): 0.80, no interval. DECODE n = 161 (Figure 1: 189 enrolled minus 20 illiterate minus 8 with insufficient data); the class split is in a supplementary table, so it is derived from the SVC's printed accuracy 0.75, recall 0.89 and precision 0.72: positives P = 161*(1 - 0.75)/(1 - 0.89 + 0.89*(1/0.72 - 1)) = 40.25/0.4561 = 88.2, so about 88 MCI/73 NC. Hanley-McNeil: Q1 = 0.6667, Q2 = 0.7111, SE^2 = [0.80*0.20 + 87*(0.6667-0.64) + 72*(0.7111-0.64)]/(88*73) = 7.600/6424, SE = 0.0344, CI [0.733, 0.867]. Even at a skewed 40/121 split the CI is [0.712, 0.888].
figures.P-19: No AUC interval printed. XGBoost: training 0.959, validation 0.795, separately recruited test set 0.913; logistic 0.818 / 0.816 / 0.778. Derived Hanley-McNeil. Test set (50 MCI/301 normal), XGBoost 0.913: Q1 = 0.8399, Q2 = 0.8715, SE^2 = 11.764/(50*301), SE = 0.0280, CI [0.858, 0.968]; logistic 0.778, CI [0.699, 0.857]. Validation (8:2 split, n = 388, about 66/322): XGBoost 0.795, SE = 0.0344, CI [0.728, 0.862]; logistic 0.816, CI [0.751, 0.881].

matched_figure_check: No figure is reported in the other's population or with the other's predictors, so nothing removes the population difference. The recorded pairing (P-343 external DECODE 0.80 [0.733, 0.867] against P-19 test 0.913 [0.858, 0.968]) differs both ways, but the tiers are not the same: DECODE is a separate multi-centre cohort, while P-19's test set is a second sample from the same coal mine. On the matched internal tier the gap largely disappears: P-343's 0.74 lies inside P-19's XGBoost validation interval [0.728, 0.862], and P-19's 0.795 lies inside P-343's mean +/- 1.96 SD range [0.662, 0.818], though 0.012 above the Hanley-McNeil interval [0.697, 0.783]. So the internal figures agree at least one way. On logistic regression the internal figures still differ (P-343 LR 0.73 +/- 0.01 against P-19 LR validation 0.816 [0.751, 0.881]). Condition 3 is therefore equivocal rather than clearly failed; condition 1 decides the pair.
performance_validity: Exclusion does not apply: the compared figures are 0.80 and 0.913. P-343 has 2074 participants and an external cohort. P-19's random-forest training AUC of 0.981 is an apparent training value and not a compared figure.
reason: On the recorded figures the AUCs differ beyond uncertainty (0.80 [0.733, 0.867] against 0.913 [0.858, 0.968]), although on the matched internal tier they largely agree (0.74 against 0.795). The decisive point is that they describe MCI detection in different population classes: hospitalised adults with type 2 diabetes against working-age dust-exposed coal miners, with population-specific predictors and different MCI definitions. So the pair fails condition 1, as C-180 does for the same P-19 population. C-185 repeats this comparison, because P-20 is the same paper as P-19.

The diagnosis of MCI followed the 2018 guidelines from the American Academy of Neurology, incorporating subjective complaints, objective evidence, functional independence, and the absence of dementia.
Confidence intervals were computed with the mean and standard deviation of the metrics during cross-validation.
Participants were randomly assigned to training (n = 1451) and validation (n = 623) datasets for model development and testing
Ultimately, variables including age, education, eGFR, SBP, BMI, T2DM duration, and the previously derived representation index were incorporated into model development.
Thus, the derived model is mainly applicable to the elder population with poorer glycemic control.
Workers exposed to dust who underwent health examinations at the Occupational Health Examination Center from May 2022 to October 2022 were selected as research subjects.
A total score of ≤26 is considered to indicate that there may be mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and a total score of > 26 is defined as a normal population.
A total of 1938 miners were included, of which 1607 were in the normal group with an average age of 42.642 (7.254) years

XGBoost (training set: AUC=0.959, validation set: AUC=0.795) and Logistic Regression (training set: AUC=0.818, validation set: AUC=0.816) models exhibited superior predictive performance. Results from the test set showed that the AUC of the XGBoost model (AUC=0.913) outperformed the Logistic Regression model (AUC=0.778).
